Reading a lookup failure as a transport fault skips the stage that never produced an address, and reading a working exchange as a transport fault ignores that the connection was established and the request was answered.

questions.explanation: The server demonstrably received the request and produced an answer, so every stage up to the server worked and the failure is on the way back, somewhere between that server and your network. Saying the request never arrived contradicts the answer the server produced, and keeping the fault at the server ignores a host that had already replied successfully.

questions.stem: A request from your office reaches a remote server, and server logs confirm it was answered there, but the answer never comes back to you. Other external hosts connect fine from your machine. What best explains this?
questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS

answer.exemplar: A day-long cache on the clients keeps handing out an address for a host that has already gone away, so a fault that would clear as soon as the record is corrected now lasts until each cached entry ages out, and the clients that cached it stay broken for the rest of the day. The bound that keeps the risk small is to tie the client cache to the record's own lifetime and refresh on a short timer, so the worst staleness a client can serve is about one record lifetime rather than a chosen number of hours.

questions.explanation: A complete answer ties the stretched outage to the cache lifetime outlasting the repair, and names a bound drawn from the record's own lifetime rather than an arbitrary span. Reducing lookups without addressing staleness leaves clients holding a dead address, and removing the cache entirely throws away the very benefit that made it attractive.
questions.hint: Ask what a client is still holding after the server it points at is fixed.
questions.learningObjective: judge a cache lifetime against how long a repair should stay invisible

questions.explanation: For a fixed single-server kiosk on one private network, using the address directly removes the lookup stage and with it every way that stage can fail, and the cost is that a future address change means editing the kiosk's own configuration. Choosing the name for later convenience keeps a known failure stage in the path, and choosing both while preferring the name keeps the very dependency that is the risk.
questions.hint: Ask which stages the address choice removes, and what flexibility is given up for it.
questions.learningObjective: weigh removing a failure stage against losing future flexibility

options.text: Use both and prefer the name, so a rename stays painless for staff

options.misconception: thinks a self-chosen name removes the need for any resolver
options.text: Use a name of your own choosing, so no outside resolver is involved

questions.topic: Choosing how a device names its server

questions.explanation: Each step is chosen because it eliminates one more stage for the price of one local test, running from the name the user typed, to the raw address, to the port, to a real exchange, to a second network, and only then to the far end and its logs. Bringing in the server logs early spends the hardest evidence first, and comparing networks before the local stages are exhausted multiplies the work without narrowing the fault any further.
questions.hint: Always spend the cheapest available evidence before the hardest.
questions.learningObjective: order fault-triage steps so each one eliminates a stage cheaply
